stories.summary: US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the APEC forum in Shenzhen, China, on November 19, according to White House and other officials. stories.headline: US lifts nationwide flight ground stop after four-hour air traffic control outage
stories.summary: All departing flights across the United States were halted on Friday, November 13, 2026, after a telecommunications outage disrupted communications used by air traffic control centres, prompting the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a nationwide ground stop — only the second such action in US airspace since the 9/11 attacks. The stop was lifted about four hours later, at 8:15 p.m. Friday, though airlines warned of lingering delays as they repositioned aircraft and crews. More than 5,000 flights were cancelled and over 10,000 delayed, stranding hundreds of thousands of travellers at airports. US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of anything 'nefarious' and ruled out a cyberattack, while the Transportation Secretary attributed the failure to decades-old technology. Air India issued an advisory asking passengers travelling to and from the US to verify flight status before reaching the airport.
stories.whyItMatters: The incident is a live case study on the fragility of critical infrastructure — aviation, telecom and cyber — and on how a non-cyber technical failure can cascade into nationwide economic disruption. It links directly to GS-III themes of infrastructure resilience and internal security, and to India's own air traffic management modernisation and India–US connectivity interests.

stories.headline: Microsoft apologises as global outage disrupts Outlook, Teams, Copilot for nearly 18 hours
stories.summary: Microsoft's Microsoft 365 suite, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, suffered a global outage that began on 12 November 2026 and disrupted millions of users, businesses, government agencies and airlines for nearly 18 hours, with some accounts describing a 21-hour disruption. Microsoft apologised, said it was testing fixes, rerouting traffic and boosting server capacity, and initially gave no full-recovery ETA. Services gradually came back online, but concerns remained over delayed email restoration and potential data loss. Experts and commentators described the event as a stark reminder of the world's heavy reliance on a small group of big tech providers and an urgent wake-up call for greater digital resilience. In India, business operations and airline customer support were affected, while public services in several countries also reported problems.
stories.whyItMatters: For UPSC, the outage links SciTech and governance: cloud concentration risk, critical information infrastructure, digital resilience, and the regulatory debate around Big Tech and data governance. It also provides a current example for GS-II e-governance and GS-III cyber-security answers.

stories.headline: COP31 weighs 1.5°C overshoot, 35% electrification goal and fossil fuel transition
stories.summary: Consultations on the COP31 cover decision have put three contested ideas on the table: managing a temporary overshoot of the 1.5°C warming limit, a global target of about 35% electrification of final energy use, and language on transitioning away from fossil fuels. The debate unfolds against a backdrop of war-driven energy market shocks, which have exposed how import-dependent economies can have growth, public finances and supply security held hostage by distant conflicts — strengthening the case for domestically sourced clean energy. Separately, scientific commentary warns that the oceans and land sinks which have absorbed roughly half of human carbon emissions for decades may not sustain that service indefinitely. Together the threads frame COP31 as a test of whether mitigation ambition, energy security and sink protection can be negotiated as one agenda rather than three.
stories.whyItMatters: COP31's cover decision will shape the next round of NDCs and the Global Stocktake follow-up, making overshoot governance, electrification targets and fossil fuel language directly relevant to India's net-zero-by-2070 pathway and climate equity claims.

stories.headline: Centre sanctions fresh border infrastructure in Arunachal Pradesh as China tension persists
stories.summary: The Centre has sanctioned a fresh set of infrastructure projects along the China border in Arunachal Pradesh, extending a decade-long push to build roads, tunnels and habitation-linked assets in India's easternmost frontier state. The move comes against the backdrop of persisting tension in the Arunachal sector, which has not eased despite three high-level India-China border talks held since July 2026. New Delhi frames such construction as both a military necessity along the Line of Actual Control and a governance measure for remote, sparsely populated border districts. Beijing has historically objected to Indian infrastructure activity and to renaming exercises in Arunachal Pradesh, which it claims in entirety. The latest sanctions therefore sit at the intersection of diplomacy, deterrence and frontier development.
stories.whyItMatters: Border infrastructure is the physical substratum of India's negotiating position with China on the unresolved boundary question, and it links GS-II bilateral diplomacy with GS-III border management, internal security and infrastructure.

perspectives.take: Frames the fresh sanctions as the Centre's response to a tension that has survived three rounds of high-level India-China border talks since July 2026, and explains why infrastructure in Arunachal Pradesh carries strategic weight; explanatory, Delhi-centric, no adversarial framing of either side.

static.topic: India–China boundary question and the Line of Actual Control (LAC)
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood (Bilateral: India–China)
static.whatIsIt: The India–China boundary has never been formally delimited. The two sides manage the frontier through the Line of Actual Control, a notional line whose precise alignment each side describes differently, with periodic friction at points of overlapping perception.
static.background: The dispute traces to the 1914 Simla Convention, at which the McMahon Line was drawn between British India and Tibet; China rejects that line and claims Arunachal Pradesh. After the 1962 war, India and China signed agreements in 1993, 1996 and 2005 to maintain peace and tranquillity and to build confidence along the LAC. Institutionally, the boundary question is handled through the Special Representatives' mechanism (since 2003), the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (2012) and Border Personnel Meeting points at several sectors.
static.geography: Arunachal Pradesh is India's easternmost state, sharing a long, high-altitude Himalayan frontier with China's Tibet Autonomous Region; snow, landslides and steep valleys make construction slow and expensive.
static.socioEconomic: Frontier districts are sparsely populated with thin road, power and telecom networks; infrastructure gaps encourage out-migration from border villages and leave residents dependent on limited trans-border trade.
static.whyInNews: Fresh infrastructure has been sanctioned along the China border in Arunachal Pradesh even as tension in the sector persists after three high-level India-China border talks since July 2026.
static.wayForward: Pair time-bound execution of frontier connectivity with continued diplomatic engagement through the SR and WMCC channels, so that the build-up supports rather than destabilises LAC management.
prelimsPointers: The McMahon Line was drawn at the 1914 Simla Convention between British India and Tibet; China does not accept it.
India and China signed agreements in 1993, 1996 and 2005 to maintain peace and tranquillity and to build confidence along the LAC.
The Special Representatives' mechanism on the boundary question has met since 2003; the WMCC was set up in 2012.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how infrastructure development in the Himalayan border states shapes India's negotiating position with China on the unresolved boundary question.

static.topic: Border infrastructure and border management
static.syllabusNode: Security — Border Management (also Infrastructure: Roads and Connectivity)
static.whatIsIt: Border infrastructure comprises roads, tunnels, bridges, airfields, helipads and habitation-linked assets along India's land frontiers, built mainly by the Border Roads Organisation with support from central schemes.
static.background: The Border Roads Organisation, raised in 1960 under the Ministry of Defence, constructs and maintains strategic roads in border areas. The India-China standoff in eastern Ladakh from 2020 gave fresh impetus to frontier connectivity, including all-weather tunnels and strategic highways in Arunachal Pradesh. The Vibrant Villages Programme, announced in the 2022-23 Union Budget, targets development of villages along India's northern land border to curb out-migration and strengthen frontier presence.
static.geography: The India-China border runs roughly 3,488 km across Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh, mostly through high, snow-bound and landslide-prone Himalayan terrain.
static.socioEconomic: Better roads cut travel time for remote habitations and improve access to health, education and markets, but raise questions of land acquisition, ecological fragility and displacement in ecologically sensitive hill districts.
static.whyInNews: The newly sanctioned projects add to accelerated frontier construction in Arunachal Pradesh, where China has periodically objected to Indian infrastructure activity and to the naming of places.
static.wayForward: Sequence projects so they are both militarily useful and economically durable, and bundle physical connectivity with telecom, power and habitation incentives for border villages.
prelimsPointers: The Border Roads Organisation, raised in 1960, functions under the Ministry of Defence.
The Vibrant Villages Programme targets development of villages along India's northern land border.
Border Area Development Programme funds developmental works in blocks along India's land borders.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how strategic border infrastructure simultaneously serves defence preparedness and the socio-economic development of frontier regions.

static.topic: Internal security in the Northeast and the AFSPA framework
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security (Insurgency in the Northeast)
static.whatIsIt: Internal security covers terrorism, insurgency in the Northeast and left-wing extremism, handled by the Ministry of Home Affairs, intelligence agencies, the NIA and state police, with the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act applicable in areas declared 'disturbed'.
static.background: Insurgency in the Northeast has involved multiple armed groups and a series of peace accords over decades. As violence declined, AFSPA was withdrawn from large parts of Assam, Meghalaya and Nagaland, while it continues to apply in parts of Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur and other states. Development-versus-security thinking, reflected in doctrines such as SAMADHAN for left-wing extremism, has increasingly informed policy in insurgency-affected regions.
static.geography: Arunachal Pradesh borders both China and Myanmar, giving it a dual frontier character — an external boundary with China and a porous, insurgency-linked border with Myanmar.
static.socioEconomic: Weak connectivity in the interior and along the frontiers constrains administration, service delivery and livelihood options, which in turn sustains the case for state-led infrastructure investment.
static.whyInNews: Infrastructure sanctioned along the China border in Arunachal Pradesh is framed as part of a wider effort to improve governance and security in a frontier state bordering both China and Myanmar.
static.wayForward: Combine infrastructure build-out with district-level governance and welfare delivery so that security gains are matched by visible developmental outcomes for frontier communities.
prelimsPointers: The NIA, set up in 2008, investigates terror offences under the NIA Act.
AFSPA applies to areas declared 'disturbed' under the Act, and its footprint has been reduced in parts of the Northeast as violence declined.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the development-versus-security approach in India's border and insurgency-affected regions, with reference to the Northeast.

Corporate investment has picked up, but its durability hinges on an unresolved old concern, while the RBI has given an initial nod for Paytm wallet services subject to conditions after earlier restrictions on Paytm Payments Bank. Separately, international airlines are contesting a proposed shift to Navi Mumbai, with Maharashtra's Chief Minister intervening, and Pricol promoters plan to sell their entire stake in a demerged connected-vehicle business to Warburg Pincus. In agri-business, scaling India's agri-economy is seen as dependent on compliance processes and people management alongside technology.

static.topic: RBI, Monetary Policy and Inflation Management
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy
static.whatIsIt: The Reserve Bank of India is India's central bank, established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949 under the RBI Act, 1934. It conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which has an inflation-targeting mandate of 4% CPI with a ±2% band.
static.background: The MPC framework emerged from the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act. The RBI uses repo and reverse repo rates, MSF, CRR, SLR and open market operations, while also regulating banks, managing forex reserves and acting as banker to the government.
static.socioEconomic: Inflation affects household purchasing power and savings, while monetary policy transmission influences borrowing costs for firms and consumers. Regulatory decisions on digital payment entities affect financial inclusion and trust.
static.whyInNews: The RBI's state securities auction, its initial nod for Paytm wallet services with conditions, and commentary on rising inflation have brought monetary policy and financial regulation into focus.
static.wayForward: Maintain inflation-targeting credibility, improve monetary transmission, and ensure robust regulatory compliance in digital payments while supporting innovation.
prelimsPointers: Repo is the rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
The MPC has six members: three from RBI (including the Governor as chair) and three external; the Governor has a casting vote.
India's inflation target is 4% CPI, with a band of 2–6%, reviewed every five years.

static.topic: Fiscal Federalism and State Government Borrowing
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union where powers are divided between the Union and States through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists in the Seventh Schedule, with residuary powers vested in the Union under Article 248.
static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre-State balance. The Governor, under Article 153, is the Centre's constitutional representative and has been a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Article 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Article 201).
static.geography: State government securities auctions involve multiple states, while the Navi Mumbai airport shift concerns Maharashtra's infrastructure and connectivity.
static.socioEconomic: State borrowing through government securities supports infrastructure and development spending. Airport relocation can affect regional connectivity, investment, and passenger convenience.
static.whyInNews: The RBI is auctioning State Government Securities worth ₹23,300 crore, and a dispute has arisen over shifting international airlines to Navi Mumbai, with Maharashtra's Chief Minister intervening.
static.wayForward: Strengthen cooperative federalism, ensure transparent and sustainable state borrowing, and adopt consultative planning for major infrastructure shifts.
prelimsPointers: In the Concurrent List, union law prevails on repugnancy unless a state law is reserved for the President's assent under Article 254.
The Inter-State Council under Article 263 is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
static.mainsAngle: Assess recent Centre-State frictions over Governor's assent and fiscal devolution, and evaluate cooperative federalism in practice.

stories.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang under scrutiny over alleged Chinese honeytrap links
stories.summary: Nvidia's former chief executive Jensen Huang is facing mounting scrutiny after reports alleged he misled the company's top lawyer about a personal relationship with Chinese executive Alice Huang, whose firm Megaspeed has drawn US attention. According to the reports, when press queries in autumn 2025 and again in October 2026 turned attention to the relationship, Huang described his interactions with Megaspeed and Alice Huang as appropriate, while separately admitting to being unfaithful to his wife without disclosing details of the alleged relationship. The episode has moved from a corporate-governance question into a US national-security concern, raising questions about possible foreign influence at a strategically critical semiconductor firm. Supporters have pushed back, with Elon Musk publicly backing a petition seeking Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia. Coverage has also widened to the timeline of the scandal and to the longer history of honeytrapping as an intelligence tactic, including cases involving India and Pakistan.
stories.whyItMatters: The case illustrates how personal relationships at strategic technology firms can escalate into economic-security and counter-intelligence questions, a recurring theme in UPSC questions on internal security, corporate governance and technology sovereignty.

static.topic: Corporate espionage and economic security in strategic technologies
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Linkages between development and spread of extremism; security challenges and their management; basics of cyber security
static.whatIsIt: Corporate espionage is the theft or unauthorised acquisition of trade secrets, proprietary technology and business intelligence by competitors or state-backed actors. When a state is involved, it ceases to be a purely commercial dispute and becomes an economic-security and counter-intelligence issue.
static.background: India's legal framework rests on the Official Secrets Act, 1923, which was amended in 2023 to broaden the definitions of 'secret' and 'prohibited place'. The Information Technology Act, 2000 governs cyber offences, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 regulates processing of digital personal data. Globally, the United States has used export controls and entities-list designations to shield semiconductor technology, treating the sector as critical infrastructure.
static.socioEconomic: Semiconductor design and fabrication are concentrated in a handful of geographies, so talent mobility, cross-border investment and supply-chain interdependence simultaneously create opportunity and vulnerability for firms and states.
static.whyInNews: The Nvidia episode has been framed as a case where a personal relationship at a leading semiconductor firm escalated into a US security question, sharpening debate on insider risk in strategic sectors.
static.wayForward: Strengthen insider-risk programmes, mandate disclosure norms for senior executives in strategic sectors, and build formal coordination between corporate governance mechanisms and national security agencies.
prelimsPointers: The Official Secrets Act, 1923 is India's principal espionage law; a 2023 amendment widened the definitions of 'secret' and 'prohibited place'.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the processing of digital personal data in India.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how corporate espionage and insider threats in strategic technology sectors intersect with national security, and suggest institutional safeguards.

static.topic: Honeytrapping as a counter-intelligence challenge
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Role of external state and non-state actors in creating internal security challenges
static.whatIsIt: A honeytrap is a covert intelligence technique in which a target is drawn into a romantic or otherwise compromising relationship in order to extract information, obtain leverage, or induce cooperation.
static.background: The technique is documented across the Cold War and earlier, with intelligence services deploying trained agents — referred to in Soviet tradecraft as 'swallows' and 'ravens' — to compromise targets. In South Asia, honeytrap cases have featured in India–Pakistan espionage episodes and in Indian counter-intelligence investigations involving defence and nuclear establishments.
static.socioEconomic: Digital communication and social media have lowered the cost of targeting, widening the exposure of officials, defence personnel and corporate leaders with access to sensitive information.
static.whyInNews: Explained coverage has placed the Jensen Huang–Alice Huang allegations within the longer history of honeytrapping, including India–Pakistan cases.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise counter-intelligence training, social-media hygiene protocols for personnel with sensitive access, and faster investigation and prosecution of leaks.
prelimsPointers: Espionage and spying in India are dealt with principally under the Official Secrets Act, 1923.
Domestic counter-intelligence in India is handled primarily by the Intelligence Bureau, while external intelligence is the mandate of R&AW.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss honeytrapping as a non-kinetic security threat and evaluate the adequacy of India's counter-intelligence preparedness.

static.topic: National-security screening of foreign investment in strategic sectors
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Effects of liberalisation on the economy; changes in industrial policy and their effects on industrial growth
static.whatIsIt: National-security screening of foreign investment is the practice of reviewing inbound capital in sensitive sectors — defence, telecom, semiconductors, critical infrastructure and data — to prevent foreign control or influence over assets vital to security.
static.background: India liberalised FDI progressively after 1991. Press Note 3 of 2020 required government approval for investments from entities of countries sharing a land border with India. The United States operates the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), which reviews transactions for national-security risk.
static.socioEconomic: Screening can deter capital and slow technology transfer, while under-regulation can expose critical infrastructure; the design challenge is a risk-based, predictable and time-bound process.
static.whyInNews: The Nvidia case has renewed debate on how far strategic technology firms should be insulated from foreign influence and on the role of corporate leadership in that calculus.
static.wayForward: Adopt risk-based and transparent screening with clear timelines, protect critical infrastructure and data, and align investment review with export-control and data-governance regimes.
prelimsPointers: Press Note 3 (2020) mandates government approval for FDI from countries sharing a land border with India.
CFIUS is the United States body that reviews foreign investments for national-security risk.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the balance between FDI liberalisation and national-security screening in strategic sectors, with suitable examples.

stories.headline: US Senate to examine Nvidia chip export controls as tech shares slide
stories.summary: US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before a Senate panel examining the enforcement of export controls on Nvidia's advanced chips, including how the investigation was handled and the national-security implications of overseas chip transfers. In parallel, Nvidia shares fell 4.3%, triggering a fresh selloff in technology stocks as investors weighed stretched artificial-intelligence valuations against persistent inflation. static.topic: Legislative oversight and committee scrutiny of the executive
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Legislatures scrutinise executive action through hearings, questions and standing committees; in India this function is discharged by Departmentally Related Standing Committees, Question Hour and Zero Hour.
static.background: Parliament (Article 79) comprises the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; a Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111). Money Bills (Article 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha. Ordinances (Article 123) must be approved within six weeks of reassembly. Departmentally Related Standing Committees examine Bills and ministry demands.
static.whyInNews: A US Senate panel is to examine export-control enforcement and the handling of the Nvidia investigation, with the Commerce Secretary agreeing to testify — a live example of legislative oversight of executive trade and security decisions.
static.wayForward: Strengthen committee referrals and sitting days so that legislative scrutiny keeps pace with executive action; use oversight hearings to build a public record on enforcement of strategic trade rules.

static.topic: Inflation targeting and global monetary-policy spillovers
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy
static.whatIsIt: India's monetary policy is conducted by the RBI through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), with a flexible inflation-targeting mandate of 4% CPI inflation within a band of ±2%.
static.background: The framework followed the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act, 1934 (RBI established 1935, nationalised 1949). Instruments include the repo and reverse repo rates, the Marginal Standing Facility, Cash Reserve Ratio, Statutory Liquidity Ratio and Open Market Operations. The RBI also regulates banks, manages forex reserves and acts as banker to the government.
static.socioEconomic: Persistent inflation in major economies influences global interest-rate expectations, equity valuations and capital flows, which in turn affect emerging-market currencies, imported inflation and the RBI's policy space.
static.whyInNews: The slide in US technology shares was attributed to concerns over artificial-intelligence valuations combined with persistent inflation across the economy, illustrating how inflation expectations move global asset prices.
static.wayForward: Track imported inflation and capital-flow volatility while preserving the credibility of the inflation-targeting framework; ensure policy transmission to borrowers through MCLR/EBLR channels.
prelimsPointers: Repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against securities; the reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
The MPC has six members — three from the RBI (including the Governor as chair) and three external; the Governor has a casting vote.
The inflation target is 4% CPI with a band of 2–6%, reviewed every five years.

static.topic: Strategic export controls and semiconductor supply chains

static.whatIsIt: Export controls restrict the transfer of sensitive technologies — notably advanced semiconductors and chip-making equipment — on national-security grounds, and are administered through licensing regimes such as the US Export Administration Regulations and India's SCOMET list under the DGFT.
static.background: The United States has progressively tightened controls on exports of advanced computing chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment to strategic competitors, with the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security as the licensing authority. India is a member of the Wassenaar Arrangement on export controls for conventional arms and dual-use goods and technologies, and has pursued domestic semiconductor manufacturing through the India Semiconductor Mission and related incentive schemes.
static.geography: Global semiconductor value chain concentrated in East Asia; India is an emerging node through new fabrication and assembly-test-mark-pack facilities.
static.socioEconomic: Chip shortages and export restrictions affect electronics manufacturing, automotive production, defence procurement and the cost of digital infrastructure, with knock-on effects on employment and investment.
static.whyInNews: A US Senate panel will examine enforcement of export controls on Nvidia chips, including the handling of the investigation and the national-security implications of overseas chip transfers.
static.wayForward: Diversify critical technology supply chains, deepen domestic semiconductor capability, and use multilateral export-control fora to secure access to dual-use technologies while protecting strategic interests.
prelimsPointers: India is a member of the Wassenaar Arrangement, which governs export controls on conventional arms and dual-use goods and technologies.
SCOMET — Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies — is India's controlled list for dual-use exports, administered under the DGFT.
Semiconductors are a strategic input for defence, telecommunications, computing and electric mobility.

stories.headline: US loses measles elimination status as cases hit three-decade high
stories.summary: The United States has reportedly lost its measles elimination status after continued transmission over the past year, according to reports carried by The Hindu and Mint. The decision is attributed to the Americas branch of the World Health Organization, which assesses whether endemic spread has been interrupted. The development coincides with the highest US measles case count in more than three decades. Loss of elimination status marks a reversal for a country that had held the status since 2000. It underscores how vaccination coverage, surveillance and outbreak response determine whether elimination gains are sustained.
stories.whyItMatters: UPSC uses health-governance examples to test the role of WHO and regional bodies, vaccine-preventable disease control, and the reversibility of public-health gains.

static.topic: Global Health Governance and Measles Elimination
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance; Health
static.whatIsIt: Measles elimination status is a certification by a WHO regional verification commission that there has been no continuous endemic transmission of measles for at least 12 months in a defined region or country.
static.background: Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable viral disease. The US declared measles eliminated in 2000. WHO regional verification committees, including in the Americas, periodically review elimination status; outbreaks linked to importation and low vaccination coverage can lead to loss of status.
static.geography: United States; WHO Americas region
static.socioEconomic: Vaccine hesitancy, access to routine immunisation, school-entry mandates, and public-health infrastructure affect elimination sustainability.
static.whyInNews: Reports say the US has lost its measles elimination status after continued transmission and a three-decade-high case count.
static.wayForward: Sustain high two-dose MMR coverage, strengthen surveillance and rapid outbreak response, counter vaccine misinformation, and ensure equitable access to immunisation.
prelimsPointers: Measles is a highly contagious viral disease prevented by two doses of MMR vaccine.
WHO's Americas regional office is PAHO; elimination requires interruption of endemic transmission for at least 12 months, not zero cases.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how vaccine hesitancy and weak surveillance can reverse disease-elimination gains, and evaluate the role of WHO regional bodies in global health governance.

prelims: The US had held measles elimination status since 2000; reports say it has now lost it.

stories.mainsQuestion: The loss of measles elimination status by the United States shows that public-health gains are reversible. Discuss the role of vaccination coverage, surveillance and WHO regional mechanisms in sustaining disease elimination, with lessons for India.

stories.headline: SpaceX Starship aborts booster catch, splashes down in ocean
stories.summary: SpaceX launched its Starship vehicle in a high-profile test aimed at recovering both rocket stages—a 'double catch'—to make launches faster, more frequent and cheaper. The booster catch was aborted, and the booster instead splashed down in the ocean. The mission still tested recovery and re-entry systems, but the outcome was a setback for the immediate goal of catching the booster. The test underscores both the ambition and technical difficulty of rapid reusability in commercial spaceflight.
stories.whyItMatters: UPSC GS-III Science & Technology: reusable launch systems, commercialisation of space, and private-sector participation are key areas; the event also links to space governance and debris concerns.

perspectives.take: Frames the launch as SpaceX's boldest test yet, focusing on the economic promise of a double-catch recovery system for faster, frequent and cheaper launches.

static.background: Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite. Chandrayaan-3 soft-landed near the lunar south pole in 2023. Mangalyaan (2013) reached Mars orbit on its first attempt. Gaganyaan is India's first crewed mission.
static.geography: India
static.socioEconomic: Space applications support communications, weather forecasting, disaster management, agriculture and governance; private participation aims to expand the space economy and jobs.
static.whyInNews: SpaceX's Starship test highlights reusable launch and commercial space trends, relevant to India's own private space reforms and launch competitiveness.
static.wayForward: Strengthen reusable launch technology, expand IN-SPACe/NSIL roles, and build international partnerships while ensuring space debris mitigation.

static.background: India is a founder of the Outer Space Treaty framework; UN COPUOS governs space law. Growing commercial launches have raised concerns over orbital congestion and debris.
static.socioEconomic: Space debris and orbital congestion affect satellite services, insurance costs and sustainable access to space for all countries.
static.whyInNews: SpaceX's Starship test and aborted booster catch highlight rapid reusability and the need for debris mitigation and traffic coordination.
static.wayForward: Strengthen international norms on space traffic management, debris mitigation, and transparency among state and private actors.

stories.headline: Delhi Yamuna PR and AIIMS toxic-air waits expose pollution governance gaps
stories.summary: Reports published on the same day criticised Delhi's pollution response on two fronts. Newslaundry alleged that a Delhi government 'clean Yamuna' exercise relied on temporary or cosmetic ghats and photo opportunities while the river water remained visibly filthy; a companion report described patients waiting in toxic air before they could see a doctor at AIIMS. In a South Central podcast, historian Ramachandra Guha characterised pollution as the Narendra Modi government's biggest policy failure, shifting the frame from a city event to national policy performance. Together, the reports point to a governance gap: pollution is acknowledged, publicised and litigated, yet the lived realities of river pollution and toxic air persist, with competing accountability claims between the Delhi government and the Centre.
stories.whyItMatters: Useful for GS-III pollution, urban governance and public health questions, and GS-II accountability and federalism debates over who owns Delhi's environmental outcomes.

perspectives.take: Frames Delhi's pollution response as performative, alleging cosmetic Yamuna ghats and photo ops while patients at AIIMS must wait in toxic air; report-led and critical of the Delhi government.

static.whatIsIt: Recurring winter air-quality crisis in Delhi-NCR caused by vehicular emissions, industry, dust, stubble burning and meteorological trapping; responses include GRAP, NCAP and judicial oversight.
static.background: Delhi's air pollution has drawn public-interest litigation and Supreme Court and NGT intervention for decades; emergency graded measures are invoked during severe episodes, while the National Clean Air Programme (2019) provides a city-level framework.

static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether emergency measures such as GRAP can substitute for sustained, source-specific and inter-state clean-air governance in Delhi-NCR.

static.topic: Yamuna river pollution and urban river rejuvenation
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Water pollution; Urban infrastructure — Sewage and river conservation
static.whatIsIt: The Yamuna is a major Ganga tributary whose Delhi stretch is heavily polluted by untreated sewage, industrial effluents and solid waste; rejuvenation requires sewage interception, treatment and ecological restoration.
static.background: The river rises at Yamunotri and flows through Haryana and Delhi before joining the Ganga at Prayagraj; Delhi's roughly 22-km stretch has been central to clean-up plans, the Yamuna Action Plan and NGT and Supreme Court deadlines.
static.geography: Originates from the Yamunotri glacier; flows through Uttarakhand, Haryana, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh; Delhi's polluted stretch lies downstream of the Wazirabad barrage.
static.socioEconomic: Polluted water affects drinking-water security, fisher and farmer livelihoods, public health and the river's religious-cultural role.
static.whyInNews: Newslaundry alleged that a Delhi government clean-Yamuna event used temporary or cosmetic ghats and photo opportunities while the water remained filthy.
static.wayForward: Prioritise sewage interception and treatment capacity, independent water-quality disclosure, enforcement against polluters and public participation over cosmetic riverfront events.
prelimsPointers: The Yamuna is the longest tributary of the Ganga and joins it at Prayagraj.
High BOD and low DO are indicators of organic pollution in river water.

static.topic: Delhi-NCR pollution governance and federal accountability
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Federalism, accountability, regulatory bodies
static.whatIsIt: Pollution governance in Delhi-NCR involves the Union government, Delhi government, municipal bodies, neighbouring states, CPCB, NGT and the CAQM, creating overlapping authority and accountability disputes.
static.background: Delhi is a Union Territory with a special constitutional arrangement under Article 239AA; airshed-level pollution led to the creation of the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas by a 2021 law.
static.geography: Delhi-NCR functions as an inter-state airshed spanning Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan.
static.socioEconomic: Poor coordination raises compliance costs for industry and residents and delays health-protective action.
static.whyInNews: Guha's podcast framing of pollution as the Modi government's biggest policy failure and reports of a Delhi government PR exercise sharpen Centre-state blame questions.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise airshed-level planning, transparent data sharing, clear responsibility mapping and independent audit of clean-up claims.
prelimsPointers: CAQM is a statutory body for air-quality management in Delhi-NCR and adjoining areas.
Delhi's special status under Article 239AA shapes its governance relationship with the Union.
The CPCB is a statutory pollution regulator under the Water and Air Acts.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the institutional and federal challenges in fixing accountability for pollution in Delhi-NCR.

stories.headline: US Senate Democrats press Musk on Starlink records; Congress weighs Israel aid
stories.summary: Two strands of congressional pressure on the US executive's foreign policy are converging in Washington. Democratic senators have moved to compel Elon Musk and SpaceX to preserve records concerning access to Starlink — and its military-grade variant Starshield — by Ukrainian forces, who describe the service as critical to frontline communications and drone operations against Russian attacks. In parallel, the newly assertive role of Democrats in Congress has revived a debate over whether legislative control can alter America's long-standing, largely bipartisan backing for Israel, including its military assistance and diplomatic cover. Together the two episodes illustrate how the US legislature uses oversight powers — record-preservation demands, hearings, holds and appropriations — as instruments of foreign policy, and how corporate control over dual-use space infrastructure has become a strategic variable in war.
stories.whyItMatters: Examiners increasingly test how domestic politics in the US — congressional oversight, party control, lobbying — shapes outcomes in Ukraine, West Asia and multilateral bodies where India has stakes.

perspectives.take: Frames the story as congressional accountability and war-time dependence: Democratic senators demand preservation of records on Starlink/Starshield access, with Ukrainian forces calling the service vital for frontline communications and drone operations.

Frames the story structurally: US support for Israel has been bipartisan for decades, so the real question is whether a Democrat-held Congress can or will shift aid and policy — a measured, explanatory rather than advocacy-driven account.

static.topic: US Congressional Oversight of Foreign Policy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed countries on India's interests; comparison of constitutions and separation of powers
static.whatIsIt: Under the US Constitution, foreign policy is shared between the President (Commander-in-Chief, treaty negotiation, recognition) and Congress (appropriations, Senate advice and consent to treaties and appointments, declaration of war, oversight). Committees such as Senate Foreign Relations and House Foreign Affairs can summon testimony, issue subpoenas and demand preservation of records; individual senators can place 'holds' on nominations and legislation.
static.background: The War Powers Resolution (1973) was passed over a presidential veto to reassert congressional authority over hostilities. Subsequent decades saw the appropriations power and conditional aid used as levers on policy, alongside landmark oversight episodes such as the Church Committee hearings on intelligence. Party control of either chamber has repeatedly reshaped the intensity, though rarely the broad direction, of that oversight.
static.socioEconomic: Organised lobbies and constituency politics — including pro-Israel groups and defence-industrial interests — heavily shape congressional positions, making foreign aid a domestic electoral issue as much as a strategic one.
static.whyInNews: Senate Democrats are demanding that Musk preserve records on Ukrainian access to Starlink/Starshield, while a Democrat-held Congress is being watched for any shift on backing for Israel.
static.wayForward: For India, the lesson is to build bipartisan constituencies in Congress (caucus groups, diaspora, states-level engagement) rather than relying on a single administration, since aid, sanctions waivers and technology transfers often hinge on legislative mood.
prelimsPointers: The US Congress is bicameral: 100 Senators (2 per state, 6-year terms) and 435 Representatives (2-year terms).
Treaties need a two-thirds Senate vote; the House has no role in treaty ratification.
Only Congress can appropriate funds — the principal lever over foreign military aid.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how legislative oversight in the United States acts as an independent variable in foreign policy, and what it implies for India's bipartisan engagement strategy.

static.topic: UN Security Council Veto and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global governance and reform of the United Nations
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs. The Security Council has 15 members — five permanent veto-wielding members (P5: US, UK, France, Russia, China) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. A single P5 veto defeats a substantive resolution.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and among the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for permanent expansion, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) process remains inconclusive and the African group's Ezulwini Consensus demands two permanent seats with veto rights for Africa.
static.geography: UN Headquarters in New York; the International Court of Justice sits at The Hague.
static.whyInNews: Congressional pressure over Ukraine and Israel highlights how the US uses its P5 position and aid levers together; the US has repeatedly wielded its veto in the Security Council, including on resolutions concerning Israel, which is central to the reform debate.
static.wayForward: India should keep pushing text-based negotiations in the IGN, build coalitions across the G4, Africa and L69, and pair its reform claim with credible contributions in peacekeeping, climate finance and SDG delivery.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The veto applies only in the Security Council, not the General Assembly.
India is a founding UN member and a leading troop-contributing country.
static.mainsAngle: Assess how P5 veto politics and the strategic use of aid by permanent members undermine the legitimacy of the Security Council, and evaluate India's reform strategy.

static.topic: Satellite Broadband Constellations and Space Security
static.syllabusNode: Science and Technology — Awareness in the fields of space; Security — dual-use technologies and strategic communications
static.whatIsIt: Low-Earth-orbit (LEO) broadband constellations provide high-speed internet through thousands of small satellites. Starlink is SpaceX's commercial constellation; Starshield is its separate national-security line offering secure communications and Earth-observation services to government clients.
static.background: The Outer Space Treaty (1967) bars the placement of weapons of mass destruction in orbit and prohibits national appropriation of space, but does not settle the status of dual-use commercial infrastructure in armed conflict. Reliance on commercial constellations grew sharply during the Ukraine war, prompting questions on contractual control, liability, denial of service and attribution.
static.geography: LEO operations (roughly 300–2,000 km altitude) require dense ground-station networks and spectrum coordination through the ITU.
static.socioEconomic: Satellite broadband can bridge last-mile gaps in remote regions, but raises concerns over digital sovereignty, spectrum pricing, market concentration and the risk of a private firm acquiring strategic leverage over states.
static.whyInNews: US senators' demand for records on Ukrainian use of Starlink/Starshield shows how a private operator's decisions have become militarily consequential and politically contested.
static.wayForward: India should finalise a clear regulatory framework for foreign LEO constellations through IN-SPACe and the telecom regulator, with security-audited gateways, indigenous capacity (OneWeb-type partnerships, NavIC-backed services) and a doctrine on dual-use space assets.
prelimsPointers: Starlink is a SpaceX LEO broadband service; Starshield is its military/national-security variant.
The Outer Space Treaty, 1967 prohibits WMD in orbit and national appropriation of space.
IN-SPACe is India's single-window regulator-promoter for private space activities.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the strategic and regulatory challenges posed by private dual-use satellite constellations for national security, with reference to India's emerging space-sector reforms.

prelims: Starlink is SpaceX's commercial LEO broadband constellation; Starshield is its military-grade counterpart used for secure government communications.
The US Congress is bicameral — 100 Senators and 435 Representatives — and alone holds the power to appropriate foreign military assistance.
The 2016 US–Israel Memorandum of Understanding committed $38 billion in military assistance over FY2019–FY2028, reflecting the institutional depth of the partnership.
The Outer Space Treaty (1967) bars weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not clearly regulate commercial dual-use infrastructure in conflict.
stories.mainsQuestion: The growing use of privately owned dual-use space infrastructure in armed conflict, alongside legislative assertiveness in the United States, is reshaping the conduct of foreign policy. Examine, with reference to Ukraine and West Asia, and assess the implications for India.

stories.headline: Amaravati Quantum Valley pins deep-tech hub hopes on IBM quantum system
stories.summary: Andhra Pradesh is building Amaravati Quantum Valley as a state-anchored deep-tech cluster, with a stated ambition of placing Amaravati among the world's top five quantum hubs by 2030 alongside Chicago, Munich, Singapore and Australia. The state's approach has begun with regulation and policy design before hardware, and the first major test of that blueprint is the installation of an IBM Quantum System, shipped from the United States, scheduled at the valley on February 3, 2027. Alongside the imported system, homegrown work is already emerging from the Amaravati 1Q and Amaravati 1S laboratories, indicating a twin-track strategy of foreign platform access plus indigenous research capacity. The project is being watched as a template for how Indian states can plug into the national quantum mission architecture and build talent pipelines rather than only procuring machines.
stories.whyItMatters: Quantum technology is a frontier area where India is a late but fast-moving entrant; state-level clusters like Amaravati show how National Quantum Mission goals translate into infrastructure, talent and industry linkages. For UPSC, it links Science & Technology policy, federalism in research funding, and strategic autonomy in critical and emerging technologies.

perspectives.take: Frames the story around policy sequencing — regulation and talent-building first, with Amaravati benchmarked against Chicago, Munich, Singapore and Australia as global quantum hubs by 2030.
Frames the story around hardware and indigenous capability — the IBM Quantum System's arrival as the first real test, alongside early outputs from the Amaravati 1Q and 1S labs.

static.topic: National Quantum Mission
static.syllabusNode: Science and Technology — Developments and their applications and effects in everyday life; indigenisation and development of new technology
static.whatIsIt: An apex national mission approved by the Union Cabinet in April 2023 and coordinated by the Department of Science and Technology, aimed at building end-to-end quantum capability in computing, communication, sensing and metrology, and materials and devices over an eight-year period (2023-24 to 2030-31) with an outlay of about ₹6,004 crore.
static.background: It followed earlier DST-led efforts such as the QuEST (Quantum Enabled Science and Technology) initiative and dedicated fellowships that seeded quantum research groups in Indian institutions. The mission institutionalised this through thematic hubs anchored in academic and research institutions, with targets spanning intermediate-scale quantum computers, satellite-based secure quantum communication, sensitive magnetometers and atomic clocks, and indigenous quantum materials.
static.geography: Four thematic hubs are distributed across Indian institutions; state-level clusters such as Amaravati Quantum Valley in Andhra Pradesh are emerging as complementary regional nodes.
static.socioEconomic: The mission is positioned as a talent and deep-tech entrepreneurship play — creating research jobs, startup ecosystems and skills pipelines, while raising concerns about brain drain and the concentration of capacity in a few institutions.
static.whyInNews: Andhra Pradesh's Amaravati Quantum Valley, with an IBM Quantum System scheduled for installation on February 3, 2027, is being projected as an early state-level test of the national quantum ambition.
static.wayForward: Link state clusters formally to mission hubs, fund shared cryogenic and fabrication infrastructure, build undergraduate-to-PhD talent pipelines, and pair hardware access with a clear intellectual property and indigenisation roadmap.
prelimsPointers: National Quantum Mission was approved by the Union Cabinet in April 2023 with an outlay of about ₹6,004 crore for eight years (2023-24 to 2030-31).
It is coordinated by the Department of Science and Technology and covers four verticals: quantum computing, quantum communication, quantum sensing and metrology, and quantum materials and devices.
It succeeded the earlier DST QuEST initiative that funded quantum research groups in Indian institutions.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the National Quantum Mission's hub-and-cluster design interacts with state-led initiatives such as Amaravati Quantum Valley, and assess whether India's quantum strategy is over-weighted towards hardware procurement relative to talent and component indigenisation.

static.topic: Quantum computing: fundamentals, applications and strategic stakes
static.syllabusNode: Science and Technology — Information Technology, computers, robotics; awareness in the fields of IT and emerging technologies
static.whatIsIt: Quantum computing uses quantum-mechanical properties — superposition and entanglement of qubits — to process certain classes of problems far faster than classical computers, with applications in cryptography, materials and drug discovery, optimisation, logistics and financial modelling.
static.background: The field traces to Richard Feynman's 1980s argument that quantum systems are best simulated by quantum machines, followed by landmark algorithms such as Shor's (factoring, threatening RSA-type encryption) and Grover's (search speed-up). Progress has been paced by error correction and coherence challenges, with current machines described as noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.
static.socioEconomic: Quantum capability is treated as a strategic and economic asset: it affects encryption and national security, industrial competitiveness in pharmaceuticals and materials, and the future demand for a specialised scientific workforce.
static.whyInNews: The installation of an IBM Quantum System at Amaravati Quantum Valley is India's most visible step towards hosting a commercial-grade quantum computer platform.
static.wayForward: Invest in quantum error correction and cryogenics, migrate critical systems towards post-quantum cryptography standards, and build application-level partnerships with industry so that hardware access converts into usable solutions.
prelimsPointers: A classical bit is 0 or 1; a qubit can exist in superposition, and multiple qubits can be entangled.
Shor's algorithm threatens public-key cryptosystems such as RSA, which is why post-quantum cryptography standards are being developed and adopted.
Decoherence and error rates, not raw qubit counts alone, are the key measures of a quantum computer's practical usefulness.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the strategic and security implications of quantum computing for India, and evaluate whether the country's current approach adequately balances hardware access, indigenous research and cryptographic preparedness.

prelims: An IBM Quantum System, shipped from the United States, is scheduled for installation at Amaravati Quantum Valley on February 3, 2027.

Homegrown research outputs are reported from the Amaravati 1Q and Amaravati 1S laboratories, indicating a twin-track strategy of imported platforms plus indigenous work.
The National Quantum Mission (Cabinet approval, April 2023; about ₹6,004 crore; DST-coordinated) is the national policy frame within which such state clusters operate.
stories.mainsQuestion: State-led deep-tech clusters such as Amaravati Quantum Valley are being projected as templates for India's quantum ambitions. stories.headline: Delhi-NCR bomb threats traced to 20 lakh fake email IDs, cross-border buyers
stories.summary: An investigation into bomb threats targeting Delhi-NCR has traced the operation to a network using around 20 lakh fake email IDs. The trail reportedly extends to buyers across borders and includes a Kanpur link. The case points to the growing use of cyber-enabled hoaxes and bulk fake accounts to trigger security alarms. It also raises questions about platform verification, cross-border cyber coordination, and data governance.
stories.whyItMatters: Important for GS-III internal security and GS-II governance: shows how cyber-enabled threats, fake digital identities, and cross-border networks challenge India's security and data-governance frameworks.

perspectives.take: Frames the probe as a cross-border cyber-enabled threat network, highlighting the scale of fake email IDs and a Kanpur link.

static.topic: Cyber-Enabled Internal Security Threats
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security; Cyber Security
static.whatIsIt: Internal security covers terrorism, left-wing extremism, insurgency in the Northeast, and cyber/economic security, handled via the MHA, IB, NIA and state police.
static.background: Naxalism peaked in the 'Red Corridor'; SAMADHAN doctrine guides counter-LWE. AFSPA applies to disturbed areas. The Integrated Command and Control Centres and NATGRID support cyber security.

static.topic: Data Governance and Fake Digital Identities
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance & Data; Data Protection
static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure — Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker — is a layered, interoperable stack. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data processing.
static.background: Aadhaar (UIDAI, 2009) is the world's largest biometric ID. UPI (NPCI, 2016) processes billions of monthly transactions. The DPDP Act introduces a Data Protection Board and consent-based processing.
static.socioEconomic: Fake email IDs and cross-border misuse of digital platforms raise concerns about platform accountability, data governance, and the socio-economic cost of cyber-enabled hoaxes.
static.whyInNews: The bomb-threat probe involves bulk fake email IDs, pointing to gaps in digital identity verification and platform abuse that data governance frameworks must address.
static.wayForward: Enhance KYC and email/account verification, strengthen CERT-In and platform coordination, and implement DPDP Act safeguards without enabling mass surveillance.

DPDP Act provides for consent, data-principal rights, and significant data fiduciaries.

stories.headline: Reservoirs shrink as battery recycling and Blue Flag beaches draw focus
stories.summary: India's environmental and resource governance came into focus across five reports. static.topic: Bhagat Singh, Nehru and Bose: competing visions within the freedom struggle

static.background: Key milestones of the struggle: the Revolt of 1857; founding of the Indian National Congress (1885); Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi movement (1905); Non-Cooperation (1920); Civil Disobedience and the Dandi March (1930); the Government of India Act 1935; Quit India (1942); the Cabinet Mission (1946); and the Mountbatten Plan and Indian Independence Act (1947). static.socioEconomic: Revolutionary nationalism drew heavily from educated, often lower-middle-class youth facing limited employment under colonial rule — a socio-economic base that shaped its socialist tilt.

static.topic: Nehru's critique of the 'police conception of the state' and constitutional safeguards

static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) examined the Centre-State balance. The Governor (Article 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a recurring flashpoint over assent to Bills (Article 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Article 201). static.socioEconomic: Centralising tendencies and prolonged detention without trial have historically fallen hardest on political dissenters, journalists and marginalised groups — the core of the civil-liberties critique.

The Inter-State Council (Article 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
static.mainsAngle: Recent spats over the Governor's assent and fiscal devolution — assess cooperative federalism in practice, and the balance between security legislation and civil liberties.

static.topic: World Health Organization and global health governance
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and Health Diplomacy
static.whatIsIt: The WHO is the United Nations' specialised agency for international public health, established in 1948 with headquarters at Geneva. It sets normative standards, issues guidelines, publishes global health estimates and administers the International Health Regulations.
static.background: Created in 1948 as a UN specialised agency, the WHO works through the World Health Assembly (its decision-making body), an Executive Board and a Secretariat. Landmark instruments include the International Health Regulations (2005) and the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. Global eradication milestones include smallpox (1980) and, for India, polio-free certification in 2014. The WHO's normative authority is not matched by hard enforcement powers, and its financing relies heavily on voluntary contributions.

static.socioEconomic: Non-communicable diseases now account for a majority of deaths in India, shifting the disease burden from communicable to chronic conditions and raising questions of domestic financing, surveillance and prevention.

In India, the Fit India Movement (2019) and Khelo India promote sport and fitness, including school-level certification.
static.geography: A global phenomenon, with wide variation across regions and a consistent gender gap in activity levels.
static.socioEconomic: Urbanisation, rising screen time, unsafe or unavailable public play spaces and gendered restrictions on girls' mobility all depress activity levels; inactivity in adolescence feeds into adult NCDs and household health expenditure.
static.whyInNews: The WHO reports that nearly 240 million adolescents worldwide record no active days in a week, with only about 14% meeting recommended physical activity levels and girls consistently less active than boys.
static.wayForward: Create safe, accessible and gender-responsive play and recreation spaces; embed structured physical activity in school timetables; promote active transport and walkable neighbourhoods; and institutionalise surveillance of adolescent activity levels.

static.topic: Special Sessions of Parliament and Legislative Procedure
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Parliament (Article 79) consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. It meets in sessions summoned by the President; a 'special session' is a sitting convened outside the usual three sessions (Budget, Monsoon, Winter) to take up a specific agenda.
static.background: Article 85 empowers the President to summon and prorogue each House and to dissolve the Lok Sabha, with the gap between two sessions not exceeding six months. Special sittings have been convened for occasions such as the midnight session marking the 75th anniversary of Independence (August 2022) and the September 2023 special session that took up the women's reservation Bill and Parliament's journey since 1947. Money Bills (Article 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha, and Ordinances (Article 123) must be approved within six weeks of reassembly.

static.wayForward: Codify a minimum number of sitting days and strengthen referral of Bills to Departmentally Related Standing Committees to improve legislative scrutiny.
prelimsPointers: The gap between two sessions of Parliament cannot exceed six months under Article 85.

States such as Himachal Pradesh have announced monthly financial assistance for women alongside free electricity units, adding to a growing set of state-level cash-transfer schemes.

stories.headline: Judicial misconduct, foreign divorce decrees and bulldozer demolitions in focus
stories.summary: Several unconnected developments on the same day converged on the question of how far state and judicial authority may act without legal sanction. In Bihar, RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav accused the father of BJP MLA Maithili Thakur of land grabbing, and the Darbhanga district administration demolished a wall her family had built on a government road, even as the MLA denied the charges and cited valid land documents. In Uttar Pradesh's Kannauj, the district administration demolished a portion of a Congress leader's house for alleged encroachment on government land while he is the main accused in the murder of an advocate, reviving the debate over punitive 'bulldozer' action. Separately, a commentary revisited the Justice Karnan episode to argue that judicial misconduct has exposed two gaps — the process of selecting and appointing judges to constitutional courts, and the absence of a sanction short of removal. The Supreme Court, meanwhile, explained in a bigamy case when a divorce decree obtained abroad can be recognised in India, and an Army officer was dismissed through court-martial for outraging the modesty of a woman colleague.
stories.whyItMatters: UPSC repeatedly tests the balance between institutional independence and accountability — judicial removal, the legality of punitive demolition and the recognition of foreign matrimonial decrees are standard GS-II themes with direct constitutional and statutory anchors.

perspectives.take: Frames judicial misconduct as an institutional-design problem, arguing the Karnan episode showed the need to revisit judicial appointments and to find a sanction short of the cumbersome removal process.

static.topic: Judicial misconduct and the removal of judges
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: independence, accountability and removal of judges
static.whatIsIt: Article 124(4) provides that a Supreme Court judge may be removed by the President on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, on a motion passed by both Houses of Parliament by a special majority; Article 124(5) lets Parliament regulate the procedure, which it did through the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. High Court judges are covered by Article 217(1)(b) read with Article 124(4).
static.background: A removal motion needs the signatures of 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members, admission by the presiding officer, and investigation by a three-member committee (a Supreme Court judge, a High Court Chief Justice and a distinguished jurist). No judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court has ever been removed in India; the motion against Justice V. Ramaswami failed in the Lok Sabha in 1993 for want of numbers, and the 2017 contempt proceedings against Calcutta High Court judge Justice C.S. Karnan revived the debate on alternatives short of removal.
static.whyInNews: A commentary on the Justice Karnan episode argues that judicial misconduct has brought two problems to the forefront — the process of selection and appointment of judges to constitutional courts, and the need for an alternative to the removal process.
static.wayForward: Strengthen the in-house procedure with time-bound inquiry and reasoned outcomes, improve transparency in collegium appointments, and debate a statutory oversight mechanism — all while preserving judicial independence.
prelimsPointers: A removal motion requires 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members' signatures; the inquiry committee has three members.
No judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court has ever been removed in India.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether existing constitutional and statutory mechanisms adequately balance judicial independence with judicial accountability.

static.topic: Punitive demolition ('bulldozer justice') and the rule of law
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: judicial review, fundamental rights (Articles 14, 21, 300A)
static.whatIsIt: Demolition of a person's property by the state as an extra-legal punishment, typically of an accused or a political opponent, without due process. Such action is tested against Articles 14 (equality), 21 (life and personal liberty) and 300A (right to property), as well as against municipal and encroachment statutes.
static.background: In November 2024, in a suo motu case (In Re: Directions in the Matter of Demolition of Structures), the Supreme Court laid down pan-India guidelines: no demolition without a prior show-cause notice and a reasonable opportunity of hearing, a 15-day window after the notice, a final order by the competent authority, and videography of the demolition. The Court held that demolishing a house merely because a person is accused of a crime is unconstitutional; the guidelines do not cover unauthorised structures on public land that obstruct roads or water bodies.
static.geography: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh; Darbhanga, Bihar
static.socioEconomic: Demolition as punishment falls disproportionately on the poor and on minorities, and raises questions about the accountability of district administrations.
static.whyInNews: A portion of a Congress leader's house in Kannauj was demolished for alleged encroachment on government land while he is the main accused in the murder of an advocate; separately, a wall built on a government road by a Bihar MLA's family was demolished in Darbhanga.
static.wayForward: Strict compliance with the 2024 guidelines — notice, hearing, reasoned order and videography — and independent inquiry where demolition follows a criminal accusation.
prelimsPointers: The Supreme Court's 2024 demolition guidelines require a show-cause notice and a 15-day window before demolition.
Article 300A makes the right to property a constitutional legal right, not a fundamental right.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether punitive demolition is compatible with the rule of law and Article 21.

static.topic: Recognition of foreign matrimonial decrees and bigamy
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: personal laws, conflict of laws and recognition of foreign judgments
static.whatIsIt: Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 makes a foreign judgment conclusive between the parties, except where it was given by a court without jurisdiction, was not given on the merits, was founded on a breach of natural justice, was obtained by fraud, or sustains a claim founded on a breach of Indian law. A divorce decree granted abroad therefore does not automatically dissolve a marriage governed by Indian personal law for the purposes of a bigamy prosecution under Section 494 IPC (now Section 82, BNS 2023).
static.background: Indian courts have held that a foreign divorce decree is not binding where the foreign court lacked jurisdiction based on domicile or the applicable matrimonial law, or where the other spouse had no fair opportunity to be heard. The Supreme Court has repeatedly dealt with NRI marriages and ex parte foreign decrees; India is not a party to the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, 1980.
static.socioEconomic: NRI marriages and abandoned spouses; the vulnerability of women left behind in India.
static.whyInNews: In a bigamy case, the Supreme Court explained when a divorce decree obtained abroad can be recognised in India and when it cannot shield a person from prosecution for bigamy.
static.wayForward: Registration of NRI marriages, mandatory disclosure of marital status, and a clear statutory framework for recognising foreign matrimonial decrees.
prelimsPointers: A foreign judgment is conclusive under Section 13 CPC but can be challenged for want of jurisdiction, fraud or breach of natural justice.
Bigamy is punishable under Section 494 IPC, now Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the tension between comity of courts and the protection of Indian spouses in cross-border marriages.

prelims: Removal of a Supreme Court judge under Article 124(4) requires a motion passed by both Houses with a special majority; the procedure is governed by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
The Supreme Court's 2024 guidelines on demolition require a show-cause notice, a 15-day window and videography before any structure is razed.

stories.mainsQuestion: 'Rule of law requires that no authority — judicial or executive — be a judge in its own cause.' In the light of recent instances of judicial misconduct and punitive demolitions, examine the adequacy of existing constitutional and statutory safeguards.

stories.headline: Diabetes screening fear, silenced abuse, a cracker death and an adoption
stories.summary: A cluster of society and health reports together sketch gaps in India's protective systems. In Chhattisgarh, a two-year-old died after a 'pop-pop' firecracker he put in his mouth exploded; in Kolkata, a Delhi-based online gamer was arrested for the murder of a woman he had met during an online game. Separately, an IDF survey of 502 Indian adults found most valued diabetes risk checks but very few believed they were likely to develop Type 2 diabetes, pointing to fear and low risk perception. The Hindu also reported on the under-reporting of sexual abuse of boys in Telangana, while The Indian Express reported the inter-country adoption of two tribal children by a Gujarati-American couple.
stories.whyItMatters: For UPSC, these stories connect social justice, child rights, health-system uptake and welfare delivery — themes that recur in GS-II and in essay and ethics questions on vulnerability and state capacity.

perspectives.take: Human-interest and accident-safety framing: the cracker death as a preventable Diwali tragedy, and the adoption as a feel-good 'Surat street to US home' narrative.

Rights-and-accountability framing: leads with official survey data on diabetes, a criminal investigation in the Kolkata murder, and a reported deep-dive on under-reported sexual abuse of boys and delayed justice.

static.topic: Child Protection and POCSO
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare & Rights (child rights)
static.whatIsIt: India's child-protection framework combines the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 and the POCSO Act, 2012, with state child-protection units, Child Welfare Committees and special courts.
static.background: POCSO was enacted in 2012 after national attention to child sexual abuse; the JJ Act, 2015 replaced the 2000 law and aligned adoption with CARA guidelines. The 2019 POCSO amendment raised penalties for aggravated offences.
static.geography: Telangana (reported cases); the adoption story links Gujarat and the United States.

static.wayForward: Trauma-informed reporting, male-survivor support services, mandatory training for teachers and police, and faster special-court trials.

static.topic: Non-Communicable Disease Screening
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Health & Public Health
static.whatIsIt: NPCDCS (2010) is India's national programme for prevention and control of cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and stroke, delivered through health and wellness centres under Ayushman Bharat.
static.background: Ayushman Bharat (2018) created Health and Wellness Centres; NPCDCS provides population-based screening for hypertension and diabetes. The IDF survey adds evidence on demand-side barriers.
static.geography: Karnataka (survey reported); India-wide policy relevance.
static.socioEconomic: Out-of-pocket costs and fear of lifelong medication deter early screening; low risk perception persists even among adults who value check-ups.
static.whyInNews: An IDF survey of 502 Indian adults found 84% valued a diabetes risk check even if healthy, but only 14% believed they were likely to develop Type 2 diabetes.
static.wayForward: Community-level risk communication, workplace and primary-care screening camps, and linking screening to affordable follow-up to reduce fear of diagnosis.
prelimsPointers: IDF survey: 84% of 502 Indian adults valued a diabetes risk check; only 14% thought they were likely to develop Type 2 diabetes.

static.mainsAngle: Risk perception and fear, not just cost, are barriers to NCD screening — discuss with policy options for primary health care.
